title: Allies enter Beirut; Ottoman paper money loses value, Egyptian pound imposed
why: British authorities replaced the Turkish Treasury notes with National Bank of Egypt notes, tied to sterling, ahead of French rule.

title: High Commissioner Decree 129 gives Syria its own currency
why: Replaced the Egyptian pound with a French-franc-linked currency; the bank that issued it later became the base for Lebanon's central bank.

title: Syrian-Lebanese currency becomes legal tender, redeemable at FF 20 per pound
why: Notes from Banque de Syrie were reimbursable by cheques on Paris at FF 20 for LS 1, tying the Levant to the franc.

title: Banque de Syrie et du Grand-Liban issues first banknotes
why: First notes ran from 25 piastres to LL 100; Lebanon had coins from 1924 but no separate central bank until 1964.
actors: Banque de Syrie et du Grand-Liban

title: Lebanese pound formally separated from Syrian pound
why: Notes still carried the Banque de Syrie et du Liban name, stayed franc-linked and interchangeable with Syrian money until 1948.
actors: Banque de Syrie et du Liban

title: Lebanese pound re-pegged from French franc to sterling at LL 8.83
why: After the fall of France the currency was linked to the pound sterling; a franc link was restored after the war.

title: State starts issuing small-change notes of 5 to 50 piastres
why: Wartime coin shortages led the government to issue small notes through 1950, alongside Banque de Syrie notes.

title: Lebanese pound link to the French franc abandoned
why: The franc link restored after the war was dropped in 1949, the year of the new monetary law.

title: Syria withdraws Banque de Syrie et du Liban note-issue privilege
why: Syria set up its own central bank in 1956 and nationalised the bank's Syrian business after Suez; Lebanon kept it until 1963.
actors: Banque de Syrie et du Liban

title: Decree 13513 gives Banque du Liban sole right to issue banknotes
why: Notes of LL 1 to 250 were printed in Arabic on the front and French on the back under the Code of Money and Credit.

title: Higher Banking Commission created at BDL under Law 28/67
why: Chaired by the governor, it became the disciplinary body for banks after the Intra Bank collapse of 1966.

title: Elias Sarkis becomes BDL governor
why: He ran the central bank until June 1976, when he became president; Joseph Oughourlian served ad interim.

title: Michel el-Khoury becomes BDL governor
why: He served to January 1985 and again from January 1991 to June 1993, bridging the civil-war years.

title: Edmond Naim becomes BDL governor
why: He led the bank through the 1986-90 lira collapse until January 1991.

title: Riad Salameh takes office as BDL governor (this source: 7 June)
why: Another source in this hub dates his start to 1 August 1993; he served until 31 July 2023, 30 years.

title: Official dollar rate at its strongest, LL 2.61 yearly average
why: World Bank series shows the pound at its best against the dollar in 1973 before civil-war depreciation began.

title: Official yearly average rate reaches LL 409 per dollar
why: Up from 16 in 1985, the average shows the scale of the collapse before the 1992 peak.

title: Official yearly average rate LL 695 per dollar as war ends
why: World Bank series; the pound would average 1,713 in 1992 and 1,741 in 1993 before the 1990s stabilisation.

title: Lebanon accepts IMF Article VIII obligations
why: The country keeps an exchange system free of restrictions on current-account payments, as IMF noted in 2009.

title: Official average rate settles at LL 1,508 and stays flat to 2022
why: World Bank series: 1,508 average every year from 1999 through 2022, then 13,880 in 2023 and 89,500 in 2024.

title: IMF dates Lebanon's conventional peg to October 1999
why: IMF says the pound has been kept near LL 1,507.5 since October 1999 (other sources: December 1997 or September 1999).

title: Standard & Poor's gives Lebanon its first rating, BB-
why: Lebanon was rated speculative grade from the start and was then downgraded repeatedly until the 2020 default.

title: Credit Libanais issues first Euro CDs listed on foreign exchanges
why: Part of the post-war return of Lebanese banks to international funding markets alongside the first sovereign Eurobond.

title: Credit Libanais founded as a joint-stock bank
why: Started with one branch in Riad el-Solh Square; it later took over Continental Bank (1977) and others.

title: Ali Jammal buys Invest Bank, renamed Jammal Trust Bank
why: Founded as Invest Bank in 1963, it was forced to self-liquidate in 2019 after US Treasury sanctions.

title: Beirut Stock Exchange relaunch prepared with Bourse de Paris
why: Trading had been halted since 1983; a new administrating committee started the revival that led to the 22 November 1996 reopening.

title: Beirut Stock Exchange signs cooperation agreement with Bourse de Paris
why: A new NSC-UNIX Euronext trading system followed; in 2000 GDRs, fund shares and preferred shares were listed.

title: Al-Madina Bank collapses; BDL seizes it
why: A fraud case involving about $1.65bn in missing funds, one of Lebanon's largest banking scandals before 2019.

title: Beirut Stock Exchange launches remote trading
why: Brokers could trade listed securities from their own offices from late 2006.

title: Law 161 sets up the Capital Markets Authority
why: The CMA, chaired by the BDL governor, regulates stock exchanges and financial intermediaries.

title: Lebanese Canadian Bank to merge with Societe Generale Lebanon after US action
why: US authorities accused LCB of laundering drug-linked money; its assets passed to SGBL and it paid $102m in 2013.

title: Lebanese Canadian Bank agrees to pay $102 million in US settlement
why: Closed the 2011 US case; the bank had been a $5bn-asset lender with 35 branches.

title: Cabinet approves turning Beirut Stock Exchange into a joint-stock company
why: A 2017 decree set up BSE SAL to replace the public-institution bourse.

title: Beirut Stock Exchange market value at $20.4 billion
why: The exchange's value after devaluation of the pound; the 2019 level was $9.6bn in January 2019 by another count.

title: Banque de Syrie et du Liban reorganised as BDL takes over issue
why: Its central-banking functions moved to the new Banque du Liban; the commercial arm became SNBSL and was Lebanese-owned from 1987.
actors: Banque de Syrie et du Liban

title: Public debt reaches about $28 billion, nearly 150% of GDP
why: Post-war borrowing for reconstruction had pushed debt to this level by 2001, with growth near zero in 2000.

title: IMF concludes last pre-crisis Financial Sector Assessment update
why: IMF said the last FSAP update was concluded in 2001; a fiscal ROSC followed on 16 May 2005.

title: IMF publishes Lebanon fiscal transparency report (ROSC)
why: The fiscal Report on Observance of Standards and Codes was the main published assessment of public finance before the 2006 war.

title: IMF makes first Emergency Post-Conflict Assistance drawing for Lebanon
why: SDR 50.75 million (25% of quota) after the 2006 war, backed by the Paris III programme.

title: IMF Board concludes 2007 Article IV consultation with Lebanon
why: One of the regular annual reviews of peg, debt and banking sector before the 2008 global crisis.

title: IMF makes second Emergency Post-Conflict Assistance drawing
why: SDR 25.375 million (12.5% of quota); Lebanon has never had a full IMF-financed programme since.

title: Finance minister says debt will reach $47 billion in 2008
why: Mohamad Chatah warned of $49bn if the two telecom companies were not privatised; the sale did not happen.

title: Moody's moves Lebanon's outlook from stable to positive
why: Reflecting banking-system strength after the 2008 global crisis; growth was 8.5% that year.

title: IMF Board reviews 2009 Article IV and post-conflict programme
why: Staff noted deposit insurance of just over $3,000 per depositor and a revised bank merger law.

title: Revised bank merger law lets BDL act early on troubled banks
why: Designed to avoid bankruptcies through mergers and takeovers by sounder banks, per IMF staff. (IMF staff report completed 31 March 2009 says the law was "recently enacted"; exact enactment date not given)

title: Dollar liquidity falls for first time in 11 years
why: Between May 2015 and May 2016 the country's dollar liquidity declined, triggering BDL financial engineering.

title: BDL swaps lira debt for Eurobonds, then sells them to banks
why: IMF estimated banks made $5bn and the central bank lost $13bn in foreign currency; operations repeated until 2019.

title: Interest payments take 48% of government revenue
why: Debt service limited the state's ability to invest in infrastructure before the crisis.

title: Some banks begin curbing dollar cash withdrawals
why: Late-2018 fees on dollar cash withdrawals were an early sign of the dollar shortage later made formal.

title: Qatar pledges $500 million in Lebanese government bonds
why: Bloomberg later reported Qatar had bought part of them by June 2019.

title: US Treasury sanctions Jammal Trust Bank; BDL approves self-liquidation
why: OFAC said the bank facilitated Hezbollah banking; Salameh approved the liquidation request.

title: IMF Board concludes 2019 Article IV, urges BDL to step back
why: Directors told BDL to stop quasi-fiscal operations and build bank buffers, weeks before the October protests.

title: Central bank accused of running a Ponzi scheme
why: Critics said BDL relied on fresh borrowing to service debt; BDL replied its actions fit the 1963 Code of Money and Credit.

title: Debt about 178% of GDP, third highest in the world
why: Another source here puts end-2019 debt at 172%; the ratio was behind only Greece and Japan.

title: Banks hold $12.7bn of $30bn Eurobonds; BDL holds $5.7bn
why: Bank Audi research showed domestic holders carried most of the bonds before the March 2020 default.

title: 785 restaurants and cafes closed since September 2019; 25,000 jobs lost
why: An early sign of the dollar shortage hitting the service sector; consumer prices were up 580% by one count.

title: BDL Circular 150 sets rules for fresh-money dollar accounts
why: Decision 13217 shaped the "fresh dollar" accounts that became the exempt side of the two-tier deposit system.

title: BDL Basic Decision 13221 (Circular 151) lets customers take dollars in lira
why: Banks could pay dollar balances in pounds, later at 8,000 (Dec 2021) then 15,000 per dollar, capped monthly.
dup_of: BDL Circular 151 lets depositors withdraw dollars in liras at 3,900

title: IMF chief sets four conditions for Lebanon support
why: Georgieva asked for state solvency, SOE loss cuts, a capital-controls law and a social safety net, days after the port blast.

title: BDL Circular 157 makes banks join Sayrafa platform
why: Customers had to waive banking secrecy for BDL and the Banking Control Commission on each transaction.

title: Decision 13335 (Circular 158) sets monthly dollar withdrawals from frozen accounts
why: Initially $400 in dollars plus $400 in lira at 12,000 per dollar; later raised to $800 plus 200 on cards.

title: Intermediate Circular 592 widens Circular 158 withdrawals
why: Added $400 monthly in lira at LL 12,000 per dollar, half in notes and half on cards.

title: BDL Circular 159 bars banks from buying dollars on the parallel market
why: Banks could only buy dollars transferred from abroad, recorded on the Sayrafa platform.

title: BDL Intermediate Circular 601 sets Circular 151 rate at LL 8,000
why: Raised the lira payout on dollar balances from 3,900 to 8,000 per dollar, within $3,000 a month per account.

title: Decision 13384 (Circular 161) pays dollar cash at Sayrafa rate
why: Sayrafa posted LL 22,700 per dollar when the market rate was 28,000; first intended to last two weeks.
dup_of: BDL Circular 161 allows dollar cash at the Sayrafa rate

title: 2022 budget law takes effect, ending LL 1,507.5 for civil-servant pay
why: Public salaries had been computed at the old official rate until the 2022 budget law entered force.

title: Sayrafa at LL 30,800 per dollar while market passes 43,000
why: The Sayrafa-market gap was about 40%, versus 23% when Circular 161 began, per L'Orient Today.

title: Riad Salameh charged with money laundering and illicit enrichment in Lebanon
why: Over alleged embezzlement of $300 million from BDL between 2002 and 2015, after an 18-month investigation.

title: IMF staff report puts financial-system losses near $70 billion
why: More than 300% of 2022 GDP, from exchange rate, loans, public debt restructuring and BDL operations.

title: IMF Board concludes 2023 Article IV; says restructuring is key
why: Directors urged upfront loss recognition, small-depositor protection and reform of the banking secrecy law.

title: Intermediate Circular 673 sets Circular 151 payout at LL 15,000 per dollar
why: Monthly cap of $1,600 per account in this version; the decision ran to 31 December 2023.

title: US, UK and Canada sanction Salameh on 10 August
why: France, Germany and Luxembourg were investigating about $330 million; Interpol notices were issued in May 2023.
dup_of: US, UK and Canada sanction Salameh

title: Decision 13611 (Circular 166) pays pre-June-2023 dollar deposits slowly
why: Up to $15,200 moved to sub-accounts; those who bought $100,000+ on Sayrafa were excluded unless they paid the tax.

title: Law 324 (2024 budget) taxes Sayrafa profits under Article 93
why: The exceptional tax later became a condition for Circular 166 payouts; the finance ministry set a 15 January 2026 deadline.

title: Cabinet policy statement commits to a new IMF programme
why: Reuters said the government would negotiate with the IMF and address the default; Finance Minister Jaber expected a March mission.

title: Lebanon presents unified reform vision at IMF-World Bank Spring Meetings
why: Finance Minister Jaber and BDL Governor Souaid attended; Lebanon also sought a $1bn World Bank reconstruction loan.

title: Jaber hopes to meet foreign bondholders within a year
why: The creditor group reportedly held a blocking stake above 25% across several Eurobonds.

title: BLOM Bond Index rises to its highest since the 2020 default
why: Reform hopes, including bank resolution, lifted Eurobond prices to post-default highs.

title: IMF mission visits Beirut on banking reform and the 2026 budget
why: Staff called the Bank Resolution Law a good start needing amendments; the mission ended 25 September.

title: Intermediate Circulars 746/747 raise monthly deposit repayments from December 2025
why: Circular 158: $1,000 a month; Circular 166: $500; annual caps $11,000 and $5,500 for the cycle to 30 June 2026. Circular 746 = Intermediate Decision 13770 of 28 Nov 2025, effective 1 Dec 2025 (BDL Circular 158 text); Circular 747 not separately confirmed.

title: Finance ministry orders payment of tax on Sayrafa profits
why: Taxpayers above $15,000 in 2021-23 had to pay by 15 January 2026 or face referral to the financial prosecutor.

title: Salameh case reported moving to Lebanon's highest criminal court
why: The central bank embezzlement case was reported in January 2026 as being sent to the highest criminal court.

title: BDL issues Intermediate Circulars 768 and 769 on dollar deposit repayments
why: The latest in a series of renewals of Circular 158 and 166 schemes; this listing does not give the changed amounts. Circular 768 is Intermediate Decision 13824 of 4 June 2026, effective 1 July 2026 (BDL Circular 158 text); Circular 769 not separately confirmed.

title: Lebanon picks Alvarez and Marsal for a new BDL audit
why: New audit would cover transactions from 1 October 2019 to 31 December 2023.

title: Extra deposit payments added for Oct 2024 to Jan 2025
why: Circular 158 and 166 holders who signed the secrecy waiver by set dates got extra monthly payments.

title: EEC and Lebanon sign cooperation agreement in Brussels
why: The 1977 agreement was replaced by the 2002 Association Agreement once it entered into force in 2006.

title: Lebanon and EFTA sign Declaration on Cooperation
why: First step toward the free trade agreement concluded in 2004 with Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

title: Greater Arab Free Trade Area tariff phase-out begins
why: Lebanon joined in 1997; tariffs fell 10% a year, with full free trade in January 2005 (as reported by official trade pages).

title: Greater Arab Free Trade Area reaches full tariff removal
why: Gradual cuts from 1998 ended; Lebanon's earlier bilateral Arab free trade agreements were absorbed into GAFTA.

title: Lebanon formally applies for WTO accession
why: The application preceded the 14 April 1999 working party; Lebanon has observer status, not membership.

title: Cabinet adopts WTO Accession Master Plan; Economy ministry leads
why: The plan assessed reforms needed for WTO conformity; a WTO unit followed in May 2001.

title: Lebanon presents Memorandum on Foreign Trade Regime to WTO
why: The MFTR covered all aspects of Lebanon's trade and legal regime and started the Geneva question rounds.

title: First WTO working party meeting on Lebanon in Geneva
why: Later meetings: 4 Dec 2003, 8 Jul 2004, 3 Mar 2006, 3 May 2007 (fifth) and a seventh in October 2009.

title: Lebanon submits initial WTO market-access offers on goods and services
why: Revised offers followed in June 2004 and again in 2007 on a bilateral basis.

title: EFTA-Lebanon free trade negotiations launched in Beirut
why: Talks ended in Montreux on 24 June 2004 after three rounds.

title: EFTA-Lebanon free trade agreement concluded at Montreux
why: Asymmetric tariff dismantling: EFTA at entry into force, Lebanon from 2008 to 2015; notified to the WTO in 2007.

title: EU-Lebanon Association Agreement enters into force
why: Signed in June 2002; Lebanese industrial and most farm goods gained free access to the EU, phased in over 2008-2014.

title: Fifth WTO working party meeting moves Lebanon to draft report stage
why: The working party began preparing its draft report; bilateral talks with members took place on 2 and 4 May.

title: Seventh and last WTO working party meeting on Lebanon
why: WTO lists no later meeting; a 2022 WTO paper puts Lebanon among accessions needing reactivation.

title: Lebanon-Turkey association agreement signed but not ratified
why: A free trade area over ten years; a regional council with Syria and Jordan stalled after the Syrian war.

title: Lebanon loses EU GSP treatment because of its free trade agreement
why: Countries with preferential FTA access stopped benefiting from the EU Generalised Scheme of Preferences.

title: Lebanon signs pan-Euro-Mediterranean origin Convention
why: Ratification was still pending in the EU's trade page.

title: Lebanon opens free trade talks with MERCOSUR
why: No agreement followed; this US commerce guide lists the launch only.

title: Lebanon joins the Agadir Agreement
why: Joined with Palestine; Agadir gives tariff-free trade among Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Tunisia.

title: WTO lists Lebanon among accessions needing reactivation
why: Last working party was October 2009; Lebanon's application dates from 1999.

title: Decree 7968 creates the Lebanese Petroleum Administration
why: Implemented Law 132/2010; the board was appointed by Decree 9438 on 4 December 2012.

title: Decree 9438 appoints the Petroleum Administration board
why: The LPA became operational to run the first licensing round.

title: Energy minister opens first pre-qualification round for oil companies
why: Decision 2 started the round that led to Decree 9882/2013 on qualification criteria.

title: Decree 10289 issues Petroleum Activities Regulations
why: Implementing rules for Law 132/2010 on licensing, drilling and safety.

title: Decree 43 adopts the Tender Protocol and model EPA
why: Set rules for the first offshore licensing round; amended by Decree 4918/2019.

title: LPA publishes second pre-qualification results for the first round
why: Eight new applicants were assessed; Novatek was qualified individually as a non-operator.

title: Bids close in first offshore licensing round after extension
why: Deadline moved from 15 September; LPA evaluation followed.

title: Cabinet awards Blocks 4 and 9 to Total, Eni and Novatek
why: The only awards from the first round; EPAs were signed in January 2018 per LPA (another source here says 9 February).
dup_of: Total, Eni and Novatek sign exploration agreements for offshore Blocks 4 and 9

title: Minister approves exploration plans; first exploration period starts
why: The consortium had submitted plans in March 2018 and committed to at least one well in Block 4 then Block 9.

title: Cabinet Decision 61 orders preparations for second licensing round
why: Led to the June 2019 launch of the second round.

title: Energy minister launches Lebanon's second offshore licensing round
why: Decision 1 was published in the Official Gazette on 13 June 2019; cabinet had approved the launch in April.

title: Minister approves drilling permit for first offshore well in Block 4
why: Drilling was planned for February 2020 after an application in October 2019.

title: Total starts drilling Byblos well 16/1 in Block 4
why: The first offshore well in Lebanon's history; it ended on 8 May 2020.

title: Block 4 well completed; no reservoirs found, traces of gas only
why: The target Tamar formation was not found; the first Lebanese well was dry.

title: Second-round bid deadline pushed to 30 April, then 1 June 2020
why: First set at 31 January 2020; requests from oil firms and COVID-19 caused delays.

title: Minister completes second round and opens all eight free blocks
why: Decision 3 set 30 June 2023 as closing date; Official Gazette issue 48 of 2 December 2021.

title: Decree 9095 amends tender protocol for second round, allowing online bids
why: Also amended parts of the model EPA.

title: Cabinet moves Novatek stake as exploration period ends 22 October
why: Novatek told Beirut it would exit; the cabinet gave TotalEnergies temporary majority control.

title: Energy minister extends second-round bid deadline to 30 June 2023
why: Later decisions of 16 November and 18 December 2023 extended the evaluation period.

title: QatarEnergy takes 30% stake in Blocks 4 and 9
why: It replaced Novatek in the consortium with TotalEnergies and Eni at 35% each.

title: Qana well 31/1 spudded in Block 9
why: The consortium's second attempt in six years; the Israel-Lebanon deal of October 2022 split the Qana prospect.

title: TotalEnergies tells Lebanon Qana well 31/1 is dry
why: Good reservoirs but filled with water; Beirut asked the company to drill again later.
dup_of: Drilling starts on Block 9 (Qana); well comes up dry

title: Lebanon opens third offshore licensing round
why: Blocks 1-8 and 10 were on offer per press reports; bids were due 28 November 2025.

title: Bids close in third offshore licensing round
why: Deadline set by Minister's decision; Block 8 was awarded to TotalEnergies, Eni and QatarEnergy in January 2026.

title: Tourist arrivals pass one million for first time since the war
why: World Bank series: 1,016,000 in 2003, up from 424,000 in 1996 and 450,000 in 1995.

title: Arrivals peak at 1.28 million, then fall 11% in 2005
Arrivals rebound to 1.33 million after two weak years
why: From 1,017,000 in 2007; 2009 reached 1.84m and 2010 2.17m on the World Bank series.

title: Tourism receipts hit $8.0 billion (World Bank series)
why: Arrivals 2.17m on the World Bank series (the ministry counts 2.35m); receipts fell to $6.8bn in 2011.

title: Arrivals fall 24% to 1.66 million as the Syrian war begins
why: Down from 2.17m in 2010; they fell again to 1.37m in 2012 and 1.27m in 2013 (World Bank).

title: Arrivals reach 1.96 million, highest since 2010 on this series
why: World Bank series; receipts were $8.69bn in 2018 and $8.72bn in 2019, the series high.

title: Tourism receipts collapse 73% to $2.4 billion
why: From $8.7bn in 2019 (World Bank) amid the financial crisis, COVID-19 and the Beirut blast.

title: Remittances jump to $4.7 billion, 23.6% of GDP
why: From $2.5bn in 2002 (13.3% of GDP) on World Bank data; the share hit 26.4% in 2004.

title: Remittances reach $7.2 billion, 24.7% of GDP
why: World Bank series; $7.56bn in 2009 (another source cites $8.2bn that year).

title: Remittances peak at $7.6 billion in this series
why: Followed by $7.0bn in 2018 when they were only 12.7% of GDP, the lowest share in the series.

title: Remittances reach 27.5% of GDP as the economy shrinks
why: $6.35bn in 2021; 30.7% in 2022 and 33.4% in 2023 on World Bank data as GDP collapsed.

title: Remittances $6.7 billion, one third of GDP
why: The share was 33.35%, more than double the 2018 level of 12.7%.

title: Real GDP falls 42.5% in the worst war year for output
why: World Bank series: GDP growth -42.5% in 1989, then +26.5% in 1990 and +49.5% in 1991 on the rebound.

title: Nominal GDP reaches $7.9 billion as reconstruction begins
why: From $2.7bn in 1989 (World Bank); it passed $17bn in 1998.

title: Real GDP grows 11.3% in 1996 despite Grapes of Wrath
why: World Bank series; 1995 growth was 6.4% there, and growth slowed to 1.1% in 1997.

title: Real GDP grows 10.2%, the best year of the post-2006 boom
why: World Bank series: 9.3% in 2007, 9.1% in 2008 and 10.2% in 2009 as banks rode the global crisis.

title: Nominal GDP peaks at about $54.9 billion
why: World Bank series; it fell to $51.6bn in 2019 and $31.7bn in 2020.

title: Real GDP falls 21.4% and inflation hits 84.9%
why: World Bank series; 2019 growth was -6.9%; inflation reached 154.8% in 2021 and 171.2% in 2022.

title: Inflation peaks at 221.3%, GDP at $20.1 billion
why: World Bank series: nominal GDP lowest in 2023 at $20.1bn versus $54.9bn in 2018.

title: Inflation falls to 45%, then 14.6% in 2025
why: World Bank series, after the pound settled at 89,500 per dollar; GDP fell 7.1% in 2024.

title: Foreign reserves peak near $52.5 billion incl. gold; $55.4bn in 2017
why: World Bank series including gold: 2012 $52.5bn, 2017 $55.4bn, then $27.5bn in 2023.

title: Foreign reserves fall to $27.5 billion incl. gold
why: From $52.2bn in 2019 on the World Bank series; they recovered to $33.3bn in 2024.

title: Reserves reach $3.0 billion incl. gold on the eve of the war
why: World Bank series: $1.5bn in 1973; $7.0bn by 1980 on gold and oil-boom deposits.

title: Reserves reach $10.4 billion, then fall to $7.6 billion in 2001
why: World Bank series including gold, matching the 2000-01 reserve losses reported elsewhere in this hub.

title: Reserves jump to $16.4 billion incl. gold in 2003
why: World Bank series: $10.4bn in 2002 to $16.4bn in 2003; the cause is not stated in the source.

title: Official yearly average rate LL 13,880; 89,500 in 2024
why: World Bank average after the 1 February 2023 reset; the 1,508 flat rate had held since 1999.

title: Bank assets exceed $75 billion; stock market value $10.9 billion
why: Wikipedia dates the figures to mid-2006; the July war then hit tourism.

title: EU ties remaining 500m euros of 1bn package to IMF deal
why: Commissioner Suica said funds depend on bank restructuring and an IMF programme.
